holding_summary: A rent-controlled tenant may not be evicted or ejected merely for charging a roommate a disproportionate share of the rent, since no rent control regulation forbids this, but where the tenant allegedly charged a roommate (and reportedly ran the apartment as an informal bed-and-breakfast for short-term foreign visitors) more than the entire legal rent, the landlord may still pursue injunctive relief and damages for profiteering. The court dismissed the declaratory-judgment and ejectment claims while allowing the profiteering-based injunction and disgorgement claims to proceed.

quotes.text: while defendant may not be evicted or ejected under the circumstances alleged herein, plaintiff may still seek injunctive relief enjoining defendant from profiteering and damages resulting from that purported conduct.

Plaintiff alleges in its papers that the building staff noticed that there were many individuals who appeared to be traveling from foreign countries who, on a continual basis, would stay for a few days or weeks in the apartment.

notes: Characterization left null: the court resolved rent-profiteering and roommate-law questions, not the lease/license/lodging character of the short-term arrangement. who_was_letting left unclear because the letter was a rent-controlled tenant, not an owner/householder, and it is unclear whether she resided alongside the transient occupants.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: The City's informal, unwritten arrangement to place homeless families in a motel's rooms at a fixed daily rate did not create a de facto lease requiring ULURP review, because the motel's owner retained possession and control, remained free to end referrals, and treated placed families the same as any other guests rather than surrendering the property. The court reversed the order compelling ULURP and fair-share review and dismissed the proceeding.

holding_summary: In summary proceedings to remove welfare recipients placed day-to-day in a motel's rooms, the court declined to resolve whether the occupants were tenants or innkeeper's guests, holding instead that the motel could not proceed under the summary eviction statute without alleging and proving whatever notice the Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law requires for the applicable relationship. The petitions were dismissed without prejudice for failure to plead or prove such notice.

quotes.text: The petitions are dismissed without prejudice. The petitions contain no allegation nor was there any proof of any notice having been given pursuant to any of the provisions of the Beal Property Actions and Proceedings Law.

at common law, a person engaged in a public calling, such as an innkeeper or common carrier, was held to be under a duty to the general public and was obliged to serve, without discrimination, all who sought service.

notes: Characterization left null: the court expressly declined to decide whether the relationship was landlord-tenant or innkeeper-guest, resolving the case on notice grounds instead.
